sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
A minimizer is a feasible point whose objective value is as small as the comparison set you named. If the comparison set is the whole feasible region, the point is a global minimizer. If the comparison set is the feasible part of some ball around the point, the point is a local minimizer. Every global minimizer is local. The converse is false: a valley can be the lowest point nearby and still sit above some distant valley.

The inequality can be strict or not. A strict minimizer is one that no other point in the comparison set ties. A non-strict minimizer shares its value with at least one other feasible point. A function with two isolated zeros of a square, such as a squared distance from a two-point set, has two strict global minimizers.

The infimum is the greatest lower bound of the values. It is always defined in the extended reals. A minimum is an infimum that the function attains. The argmin set is the set of feasible points where the attained value equals the infimum. That set can be empty, a singleton, or a large set, independently of whether a local minimizer exists somewhere else.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The point \(x^\star\) is a global minimizer when \(x^\star\) is feasible and \(f(x^\star) \le f(x)\) for every feasible \(x\). It is local when the same inequality holds for the feasible points of some ball. Either definition is strict when the inequality is strict for every other point of the comparison set. The optimal value is \(p^\star = \inf f(\mathcal{X})\), and
\[
\operatorname{argmin} f = \{x \in \mathcal{X} : f(x) = p^\star\}.
\]
The set is empty when the infimum is not attained.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(f(t) = (t^2 - 16)^2 + 28\). The squared factor is nonnegative, so \(f(t) \ge 28\), and equality holds at \(t = 4\) and at \(t = -4\). The shared floor is 28. Both points are global minimizers. Each is also a strict local minimizer, because a small neighborhood of one of them excludes the other and the square is positive in between.

The point \(t = 0\) has value \(256 + 28\), which is much higher, and it is not a minimizer of either kind. The argmin set has two points. Neither minimizer is strict as a global minimizer, because the other one ties it. Strictness depends on which comparison set you named.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A zero gradient is not the definition of a minimizer. It is a later calculus test, and it can hold at a maximizer. Local is not global: the cubic \(t^3 - 3t\) has a local minimizer at \(t = 1\) and is unbounded below. An infimum is not automatically a value of the function. The exponential tends to 0 and never reaches it, so its argmin set on the line is empty even though the infimum is finite. Reporting the minimizer when the question asks for the minimum value mixes a point with a number.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Existence theorems say when the argmin set is nonempty: a continuous function on a nonempty compact set, or a continuous coercive function on a nonempty closed set. First-order necessary conditions describe interior local minimizers. For a convex function the local and global notions collapse, and a stationary point is already global.
